caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Sweden's debt is low and has fallen through the period: 43.8% of GDP in 2006, a peak of 45.7% in 2014, 40.4% in 2020, 34.2% in 2022, and a projected 34.9% in 2025 (32.1% in 2023, the series low). The fiscal framework — surplus target, expenditure ceiling — is the EU's strictest, and it has delivered: COVID barely moved the ratio. GDP grew from $422.5bn in 2006 to a projected $669.0bn in 2025. Debt sustainability is excellent; the policy debate is whether the framework is too tight given investment needs.
inflation_management: The Riksbank targets 2%, and the floating krona is the absorber. Inflation was 1.9% in 2009, 0.2% in 2014 (the low), 0.7% in 2020, then 8.1% in 2022, the series high, on energy. It fell to 2% in 2024 and is projected at 2.6% for 2025 — near target. The Riksbank was among the first to hike and among the first to cut; the krona's weakness in 2022-23 complicated the fight by importing inflation. The distinctive Swedish feature is the housing market's sensitivity to rates, which made the hiking cycle unusually potent domestically.

key_events.event: Financial crisis: Sweden's 1990s-crisis-tested framework handled the shock; debt barely rose.
Negative rates era: the Riksbank went below zero (2015) to fight deflation risk.
COVID-19: the light-touch strategy; debt at 40.4% of GDP, barely moved.
Energy shock inflation of 8.1%; the Riksbank hiked aggressively as the krona weakened.
NATO accession (March 2024) ended two centuries of non-alignment; defense spending rose.

outlook_next_decade: Sweden's outlook is strong: minimal debt, a credible framework, and a diversified, innovative economy. NATO membership adds defense spending but also industrial opportunities. The structural questions are housing-market vulnerability to rate cycles and the krona's chronic weakness, which flatters exports but imports inflation. Inflation should stay near target. The analytical assessment: one of Europe's soundest macro positions, with the fiscal framework's tightness as the main self-imposed constraint.
